briefing.headline: Climate courts, party splits and devolution drama dominate politics
briefing.overview: Supreme Court hears a climate liability case while UK parties wrestle over cooperation. In Stormont a no‑confidence vote fails, and US midterms heat up.

stories.title: Supreme Court hears climate liability case
stories.what_happened: Justices heard arguments on whether energy firms can be held liable for climate change impacts in Boulder, Colorado. The case could set precedent for community lawsuits against industry.
stories.why_it_matters: The case illustrates judicial power to shape policy, a key point in A‑level study of the US Constitution and courts. It also raises questions about the balance of powers.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Holding companies accountable would force faster emissions cuts and protect vulnerable communities.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Judges should not create policy; Parliament should legislate on climate issues.

key_term.definition: Courts examining the legality of actions by the other branches of government.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence when discussing the role of the US judiciary in policy making in a Constitution essay.

stories.title: Labour rules out coalition with Greens
stories.what_happened: Senior Labour figures said a partnership with the Green Party is unlikely after the Greens voted that "Zionism is racism". Both parties dismissed the idea of formal cooperation.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows party strategy and the impact of ideological disputes on coalition possibilities, relevant to the AQA topic of political parties and coalition building.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Labour sees the Greens' stance as incompatible with its own anti‑racism commitments.

perspectives.label: From the right
perspectives.text: Critics say Labour is missing an opportunity to unite progressive forces against the Conservatives.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Maintaining clear party identities protects voter trust.

key_term.definition: An alliance of two or more parties to form a government or achieve common goals.

stories.exam_use: Cite when evaluating why parties may choose to cooperate or stay separate in an essay on party politics.

stories.title: Stormont no‑confidence motion fails
stories.what_happened: A motion of no confidence in Northern Ireland's agriculture minister was defeated, with 38 against and 32 in favour. The vote kept the minister in post.
stories.why_it_matters: Illustrates how devolved assemblies can hold ministers to account, linking to the AQA focus on devolution and parliamentary scrutiny.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: The result shows stability in Stormont and confidence in the minister's performance.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: The close vote indicates significant dissent and a need for stronger oversight.

key_term.definition: A parliamentary vote that can remove a minister or government if a majority opposes them.

stories.exam_use: Use as a case study of devolution mechanisms in a short‑answer question on the powers of the Northern Ireland Assembly.

stories.title: Democrats face hurdles ahead of 2026 midterms
stories.what_happened: NPR reported that while Democrats feel optimistic, they must contend with fundraising gaps, candidate recruitment and voter fatigue before the November midterms. Experts warn of potential losses in swing districts.
stories.why_it_matters: Highlights electoral strategy, campaign finance and voter behaviour – core themes in the AQA elections and direct democracy unit.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Progressive policies could energise the base and offset structural disadvantages.

perspectives.label: From the right
perspectives.text: Republicans argue Democratic complacency will cost them seats.

key_term.definition: US elections held halfway through a president's four‑year term, usually for Congress.

stories.exam_use: Reference when analysing factors that influence electoral outcomes in a comparative elections essay.

stories.title: Tory plan to cut energy‑efficiency rule criticised
stories.what_happened: The Institute for Government reported that a Conservative proposal to relax building‑energy standards could add £1,000 a year to new‑home owners’ costs. The think‑tank warned of climate and consumer impacts.
stories.why_it_matters: Connects parliamentary policy‑making with environmental regulation, relevant to the AQA study of Parliament’s role in legislation and scrutiny.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Easing rules will reduce construction costs and boost housing supply.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Weakening standards undermines climate targets and harms buyers.

key_term.definition: A rule made by a government authority to control behaviour.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence of how parliamentary decisions affect policy areas such as the environment in a policy‑impact essay.

compare.uk: Kemi Badenoch’s popularity is being used by the Conservatives to project confidence ahead of the 2028 mayoral election (source 87014f88b6f1).
compare.us: US midterms are shaping party strategies as Democrats grapple with fundraising and candidate recruitment (source fde2b735fc5d).
compare.insight: Both systems show how parties use individual leaders or electoral cycles to mobilise support, but the UK relies on a single high‑profile figure while the US focuses on broader campaign infrastructure.

ideas_lens.text: The Supreme Court climate case reflects ecologism’s core belief that environmental protection should be enforced through strong institutions; thinkers like Rachel Carson argue that legal mechanisms are essential to curb corporate harm.

exam_question.question: Assess the extent to which judicial decisions can influence climate policy in the United States, using recent Supreme Court cases as examples.
exam_question.tip: Structure your answer by explaining judicial power, outlining the case facts, and evaluating arguments from both supporters and critics.
